summary: This informational document shows how to use the Session Initiation Protocol and Session Description Protocol to set up a virtual private network between two peers. It extends the SDP protocol identifier so peers can negotiate the Internet Key Exchange (IKE) as part of a media session. The goal is on-demand sharing of media or applications between peers.

plainLanguage.summary: Two people on a video call can say, in the call setup itself, that they also want a private tunnel just for them. This document gives them the words to ask for it.

questions: how to set up a vpn using sip and sdp
how to negotiate ike in sdp offer answer
subtitle: Negotiate secure tunnels directly in SIP video calls.

tldr.problem: Devices want to establish secure VPN tunnels on demand during a SIP call, but they need a way to exchange encryption credentials when they have no prior relationship and may be behind NAT.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC extends SDP to let peers exchange certificate fingerprints as part of the call setup, then use those fingerprints to authenticate IKE negotiations for IPsec tunnels.
tldr.outcome: Provides a deployed method for home routers and remote clients to agree on a VPN tunnel within a SIP call, enabling secure access to home networks without fixed IP addresses.

today: RFC 6193 is an Informational specification describing a deployed use of SIP and IKE. It remains current for on-demand VPN setup in SIP-based systems where SDP integrity is assured through identity mechanisms.

sections.title: The Problem and the Solution
sections.content:
Home routers and consumer devices often want to share media and applications, but face a problem: a device outside the home cannot connect to a device inside because the home router is behind a firewall or NAT. The solution is a VPN tunnel from outside to inside, but today that requires advance setup and fixed IP addresses.

This RFC shows how to set up a VPN tunnel on demand during a SIP call. Both peers already have a secure channel in SIP (either through prior authentication or SIP identity mechanisms), so they can safely exchange the certificate fingerprints they will use for IKE, then negotiate an IPsec VPN as part of the call itself. The mechanism reuses SIP servers for name resolution and authentication, so no new infrastructure is needed.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of setting up a VPN before a call, you set it up during the call. The call itself keeps the handshake secure.

sections.title: How SDP Describes IKE Sessions
sections.content:
The RFC extends SDP's protocol identifiers so that a media line can specify ike-esp or ike-esp-udpencap, the two ways to negotiate IKE over UDP. It also defines a new attribute, ike-setup, which works like the setup attribute in RFC 4145: it tells each endpoint whether to act as the initiator (active) or the responder (passive) of the IKE negotiation.

The offer/answer exchange follows the same rules as other media negotiation: if both sides agree on a format, the endpoints then start an IKE session and validate each other's certificates by comparing the fingerprints that were already exchanged in SDP.
sections.plainLanguage: SDP adds two new words: one says 'this is an IKE tunnel', and another says 'you start it' or 'I start it'.

sections.title: The Handshake and Certificate Validation
sections.content:
Once SDP offer/answer completes, the IKE initiator (determined by the ike-setup attribute) begins an IKE session with the responder. During IKE phase 1, both peers present certificates for digital signature authentication. Each peer compares the hash (fingerprint) of the certificate it receives with the fingerprint that was exchanged in the SDP offer/answer. If they match, the IKE negotiation continues; if not, the session terminates.

The document also specifies how to handle NAT traversal: if either peer is behind NAT, it uses ike-esp-udpencap instead of ike-esp, and may combine IKE with the ICE framework. When ICE is used, STUN packets, IKE packets, and UDP-encapsulated IPsec packets must be demultiplexed on the same UDP flow.
sections.plainLanguage: The peers prove they are who they say by showing certificates whose magic numbers (fingerprints) match what was already agreed in the call setup.

sections.title: Use Cases and Conditions
sections.content:
The RFC lists several practical uses: sharing media over a home network using DLNA, remote desktop support during a customer service call, remote medical equipment monitoring, and peer-to-peer gaming. It also notes the deployment assumption: the integrity of the SDP exchange itself must be assured, typically through SIP identity (RFC 4474) or SIP connected identity (RFC 4916), so that the fingerprint exchange cannot be tampered with.

For cases where peers already have a prior relationship (trusted certificates or pre-shared keys), the document also describes how to use the psk-fingerprint attribute to exchange a hash of a pre-shared key instead.
sections.plainLanguage: This works best when you already trust the person calling you, because you verify their certificate hasn't been faked.

sections.title: Security and Limitations
sections.content:
The security of the scheme depends entirely on the integrity of the SDP exchange. If an attacker can modify the SDP offer/answer, they can swap out the fingerprint, trick the responder into accepting a different certificate, and intercept the VPN. The RFC requires that SIP identity or equivalent protection be applied to the SDP to prevent this.

The document does not modify IPsec/IKE itself; it only specifies how to trigger an IKE session and validate certificates using fingerprints. Security policy (which traffic goes through the VPN, how addresses are assigned) is the responsibility of the application, not SDP. The RFC advises against using SIP re-INVITE to maintain the VPN session; each endpoint MUST use IPsec's own keep-alive and rekeying mechanisms.
sections.plainLanguage: The security chain is only as strong as SIP's authentication. If someone tricks SIP, they can trick the VPN too.
